speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head W of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past 60 years, we have developed from Third World to First.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Transport has been a critical part of that story.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The hot and creaky public buses have been replaced by fully air conditioned ones.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We opened our first Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) line in 1987 and we now have six lines with more than 140 MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our airport and seaport are among the best in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to ask the Ministry to share how it will take Singapore's transport system forward in the next phase?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For MRT, we plan decades ahead of time with new technologies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides more express bus services and bus route adjustments, how else will we reinvent our public bus system?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have the North-South Corridor (NSC) to look forward to.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides ferrying humans by air, how close are we to seeing our goods and food deliveries flown by unmanned drones, like what is already being done in various cities in China?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the next bound for our transport system beyond SG60 and when do we expect to get there?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the six-day interruption on the East-West Line (EWL) in late September 2024 brought the issue of rail reliability back into focus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was an unexpected disruption, especially after several years of steady improvements and minimal incidents since the challenges in 2012.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A Straits Times forum letter highlighted the importance of balancing rail reliability with costs, emphasising the severe impact of extreme events on commuters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a valid concern and we must always strive to minimise disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, it is important to recognise that our rail operators are not neglecting maintenance to cut costs or simply meet performance indicators.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond their service obligations, operators bear significant expenses for service recovery, bridging bus services and repairs during major disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The EWL incident, while unfortunate, demonstrated the effectiveness of our response system and the adaptability of commuters who navigated the situation with patience and understanding.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Transport Minister has assured us that SMRT has maintained its maintenance spending, even during years without major incidents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is natural to question whether more should be spent, we must also consider the financial balance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the Public Transport Council carefully managing fare adjustments to protect commuters, any additional funding for enhanced maintenance may require increased Government subsidies, a cost ultimately borne by taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Greater transparency on revenue and cost figures could help foster public understanding of this complex equation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The timing of the 2024 disruption during the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) season added another layer of stress for affected students and parents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While such stress is difficult to quantify, it is reassuring that the School Examinations and Assessment Board acted swiftly to accommodate affected students.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reflects the strength of our broader support ecosystem, on top of what Ministry of Transport (MOT) has done, which works alongside transport operators to mitigate the wider impact of service disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we expand our rail network in the coming decade, a key question remains: what proactive measures are we taking to uphold reliability standards and develop a skilled, future-ready workforce to sustain those efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Continued collaboration, innovation and learning from past incidents will be essential in building an even more resilient rail system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us use this incident as an opportunity to refine our strategies and reaffirm our commitment to a reliable and commuter-centric public transport network.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, our MRT network is the backbone of our public transport system.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With a growing network and more rail assets to operate and maintain, we need to ensure that we have the appropriate measures in place and dedicate sufficient resources to keep our rail network available and reliable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will the Ministry share its insights on how it will enhance rail infrastructure reliability to minimise service disruptions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With an expanding rail network, with the Jurong Regional Line and Cross Island Line in the pipeline, what are the steps taken to recruit, train and retain talents for the rail transport workforce?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Taking the MRT is part of many Singaporeans' everyday life and it is hard to imagine what Singapore was like before the advent of MRT travel.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's first MRT service started in 1987 and was then just a six-kilometre stretch of the North-South Line (NSL) between Yio Chu Kang and Toa Payoh.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every day, 9,500 engineers, technicians, statisticians, schedulers and station, workers work diligently to keep our Singapore train services running, making our train services one of the most comfortable and reliable in the world.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Executive Secretary (ES) of the National Transport Workers Union (NTWU), I have met personally, the good men and women from our Rail Industry.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unbeknownst to many, no two rail systems are exactly the same and our rail engineers and technicians are passionate solvers who think out of the box dealing with tens of thousands of spare parts and multiple vendors to maintain and repair train systems uniquely Singaporean in terms of age, build, obsolescence and technical parts used.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As public transport workers, our Rail workers bear their work with purpose and national pride.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the recent MRT service disruptions, our rail teams worked ceaselessly through many late nights and early mornings, in rain and shine, to minimise train disruptions, all the time carrying the heavy weight of duty to our commuters on their shoulders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there plans by the Ministry to continue to reinvest into technology alongside our rail operators to ensure that our rail workers have more accurate monitoring gauges to pre-empt maintenance requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, an efficient and reliable public transport is vital in moving millions of Singaporeans daily.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I note from the Transport Minister's recent Parliamentary Question replies that the Land Transport Authority (LTA) was still looking into the root causes of the recent train disruptions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope the investigations would address the following areas: One, how did the recent train disruptions differ from past occurrences?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Were these technical failures, human errors, or external factors influencing the rail system?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Two, how did the LTA and our rail operators handle the train disruptions as they unfolded and how can we ensure timely and clear updates to affected commuters?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Three, will there be a review of the current training and preparedness protocols for staff in handling major train disruptions?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are there plans to implement more rigorous training and better incident response simulations to better prepare for unexpected situations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is also important that we continue to invest in predictive and preventative maintenance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also invest in redundancy systems and parallel bus routes that can be activated swiftly during disruptions, so as to allow commuters to continue their journeys with minimal impact.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While disruptions are an unfortunate reality of any transport system, they can also be catalysts for improvement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By proactively addressing the root causes, we can refine our rail system to ensure a safer, more reliable experience for all Singaporean commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Residents in Jurong West are currently served only by the East-West Line, and we welcome the upcoming Jurong Region Line, or JRL.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While Singapore's train network has significantly improved in reliability and consistently achieving over one million mean kilometres between failure (MKBF), breakdowns cannot be entirely ruled out.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will not only provide alternative routes during disruptions but also improve connectivity and convenience for residents in the western region.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the Land Transport Master Plan (LTMP) 2040 was first released by LTA in 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am concerned about the pace of progress in encouraging public transport use, given we are just five years away from 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Regardless, however, we should aim to ambitiously exceed our current car lite light targets by enhancing the affordability, comfort and reliability of our public transport network.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Commuting via public transport should be made more economical for regular commuters, especially given the high cost of car ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the adult monthly travel pass is still considered expensive by many frequent commuters, many of whom are also being squeezed by the high cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lowering the cost of the travel pass could better incentivise Singaporeans currently taking less environmentally friendly private vehicle options, regardless of whether it is cars, taxis or private hire vehicles (PHVs), to make the switch to public transport.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is ultimately our goal, as expressed by the LTA, if the plan is to meet and exceed the 75% public transport mode share.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, would the Government consider reducing the price of the adult monthly travel pass to further incentivise greater public transport use?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, could the scheme be expanded to include City Direct and Express fares as well, given an expansion of such travel options as part of the commuting mix and that these two are green public transport options as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that building a people-centric public transport network may require funding from the Government's purse, which also includes sustainability-linked revenue sources such as carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, with carbon taxes aimed at supporting our decarbonisation efforts set to increase in the future, would the additional revenue generated help fund enhancements to our public transport network?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Singapore accelerates towards a car lite future, building a transportation network centred around affordable, comfortable and reliable public transit should be the Transport Ministry's utmost priority.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, many of my residents are appealing to have MRT stations in the proximity of their homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will LTA reconsider a new MRT line to support residents at Seletar, Yio Chu Kang, Fernvale at the central, north and northeast zones to the city at the south, and new Woodlands North, as well as to Changi Airport on the east and Tuas on the west?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more Built-To-Order (BTO) flats in Fernvale, the demand for bus services has been increasing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents need the connectivity to other parts of Singapore and the waiting and commuting times should preferably be minimised as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, would LTA introduce new bus services in Fernvale under the Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme, as well as additional new bus services, once the Buangkok Drive extension is completed, to connect to Buangkok MRT and Yio Chu Kang MRT stations?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would the Government please consider either increasing the frequency of Bus Service 112 throughout the day or add an additional full-day bus service to serve Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have written appeals regarding various different residents' feedback for this bus service over the years, including frequency of services and asking for services to be increased, bus services timing on the LTA's my TransportSG app, at being inaccurate, buses not keeping to scheduling, buses bunching up and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Residents have also asked for an additional bus service to ply Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But there are only two services each during morning and evening peak periods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, resident commuters I spoke to before and after 17 February still wish for the waiting times for the rest of the day, including the evening peak times, to be reduced, as well as for a second full-day bus service to ply Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I appeal for LTA to look into reducing waiting times at other times of the day, as well as to consider my request for an additional full-day bus service along Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recently appealed, on behalf of a resident, for LTA to consider diverting one of the current bus services currently travelling from Hougang Avenue 8 Punggol Park towards the Hougang Interchange via Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One of these buses can be diverted to travel via Hougang Avenue 7, Hougang Avenue 5, before heading to Hougang Interchange.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: LTA has said in a recent reply to my appeal letter on behalf of a resident that diverting could result in longer travel times and higher fares for onboard passengers, as well as affect connectivity for commuters at bus stops along Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Respectfully, such a proposal will only add one more additional bus stop to any of the four bus services as compared with the current route along Upper Serangoon Road but will cater to serve a greater number of residents living along Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, there are already a number of such services plying Upper Serangoon Road before heading towards Hougang Interchange.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will urge LTA to balance the interest of Hougang Avenue 7 commuters, who have only one such full-day service, as opposed to various existing full-day services along Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: LTA also suggested in a reply to my appeal letter on behalf of a resident that Hougang Avenue 7 residents are within a 400-metre walk to bus services plying Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Sadly, such a walk may not be expedient for many of our seniors, or those with mobility issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, Bus Service 112 is a long loop service between Hougang Interchange, Hougang Avenue 7, Tampines Road, Kovan, Upper Serangoon Road, Hougang Avenues 2, 8, 9 and 10 and Hougang Street 92.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I took a ride on Bus Service 112 recently in the afternoon, and it took me more than one hour and 10 minutes for the loop.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am not surprised that the nature of this long greater Hougang loop service contribute to the bunching, especially during peak times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A diversion from one of the four above mentioned buses, or better still, a direct feeder bus service alongside Bus Service 112, will provide a more direct access for residents along Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Today, with the same purpose of enhancing the public service for my residents, I would like to request the extension of Bus Service 137 to one of the loops of Bedok South Street 3.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The bus route covers Bedok North Avenue 1, Bedok North Avenue 2, Bedok North Street 3 of Kaki Bukit ward.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, the route from Sims Place to Upper East Coast direction does not cover the loop of Bedok North Street 3, which has the bus stop number 84381 and 84391.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The proposed extension will not only ease the plight of elderly residents who currently have to walk a distance to the nearest bus stop but will also lay the ground for the future residents who will occupy a potential future residential development at the former Bedok Town Secondary School.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, our public bus network serves an essential role in enhancing point-to-point connectivity for commuters who need to or choose to travel on public transport.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Encouraging more Singaporeans and residents to use public transport whenever possible is in line with our national effort to go green and reduce our carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the Ministry's plans for enhancement in bus connectivity in 2025, especially for towns with new BTO flats and regional facilities?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will MOT improve accessibility and reduce waiting times for commuters in those areas?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Good bus connectivity requires more manpower, from drivers to technicians, to maintain reliability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will we attract and retain more talent and manpower in this sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the deployment of autonomous buses for revenue service and the implementation roadmap?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How many public transport workers, in particular, our bus captains and bus technicians, will be affected by the roll-out of autonomous buses on our roads?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What is the Ministry's plan to ensure that the affected public transport workers are suitably upskilled, reskilled and redeployed?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I urge the Ministry to work closely with the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU) to ensure a smooth transition for all affected workers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, bus captains play a vital role in our public transport system, ensuring safe and smooth journeys for commuters.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They must navigate traffic while also ensuring passenger safety and comfort.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Given these responsibilities, we must ensure that they receive the support they need.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Beyond that, how can we better recognise and support our bus captains?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Strengthening career pathways and professional development can ensure that they feel valued in their roles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A well-supported workforce leads to better quality and service and a positive commuting experience for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must continue our efforts to improve the well-being of our bus captains.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: With over 3.7 million rides a day, Singaporeans are avid bus users and rely on bus services to connect them with the last miles of their daily journeys.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As new estates are built and travel patterns evolve, enhanced connectivity and bus service frequency continues to drive the productivity measures of our bus operators.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Besides new transport infrastructure, investing in our bus captains must be seen as the heart of the matter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: It is no mean feat being a bus captain.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: It requires resilience, patience, multitasking and steely-eyed focus, at all times.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The tripartite partnership has convened several taskforces looking into the safety and welfare of our bus captains and ensuring that our bus captain role continues to be attractive to new and younger entrants.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: During the task force meetings, our bus captains gave feedback that protected uninterrupted meal breaks, reasonable runtime lengths, improved technology to enhance safety, refresher programmes and stronger legislative measures against rude, violent acts need to be looked into.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Given a growing bus network and higher service expectations demanded of our captains, what more can be done to further improve the working conditions of our bus captains and transport workers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: June alone saw a public bus run over a construction worker and other buses colliding with cars, a lorry and a trailer truck.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And it is not just the accidents that we are worried about.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The risk of aggressive driving by some bus captains, including rapid acceleration and deceleration as well as swerving between lanes, endangers passengers who are elderly or otherwise less mobile.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must pay attention to how public bus safety has changed amidst increased standing capacity in new bus models over the years, an increasing shortage of bus captains and continued recovery of bus ridership post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As our train network expands, it has become the backbone of Singapore’s public transport, with buses primarily serving first- and last-mile connections.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, some bus routes still span over two hours, connecting MRT stations at opposite ends of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Such long routes are inefficient for commuters and can lead to driver fatigue, raising safety concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, I am glad that Minister of State Murali is leading a taskforce to enhance bus safety and I look forward to his updates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Meanwhile, I urge LTA to consider new bus services that connect HDB heartlands more directly to key services like polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In Nanyang, for example, many residents traveling to Pioneer Polyclinic must walk 170 meters, almost the distance of a bus stop.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For the young and healthy, this may be manageable, but for the elderly or sick, even 50 meters can be a struggle.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I hope LTA can amend existing routes or introduce new services to better serve these residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Additionally, many bus interchanges, especially open-air ones, appear dated.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Could open-air bus interchanges be converted into air-conditioned interchanges for commuters’ comfort?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If not, how can LTA better protect commuters from extreme weather, especially heavy rain and storm?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Let us work together to make public transport safer, more efficient and more inclusive for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, in rating the quality of public transport, most commuters would consider the following factors, such as safety, affordability, connectivity, reliability, accessibility, frequency, speed and last but not least, comfort.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: All these factors contribute to our commuters’ experience, which many of us go through almost daily.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The behaviour of fellow commuters is one of the main contributors to the level of comfort experienced in a journey.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Unfortunately, there has been feedback that there are inconsiderate commuters who cause nuisance and disturbances to other commuters.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The common complaints include conversing with their friends or on their phones loudly, playing loud music, littering and dirtying seats and stations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How can the Ministry discourage such inconsiderate behaviour?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would MOT consider introducing fines and other forms of penalties for recalcitrant offenders?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Our public transport system should be a calm, reliable mode of travel for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Yet, many commuters continue to suffer from excessive noise on trains and buses, whether it is someone playing loud videos on speakers or having disruptive phone conversations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While "Hush Hush Hannah" has raised awareness, we can still move beyond mascots, reminders and courtesy campaigns to create lasting behavioural change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We can have a structured system of personal accountability, backed by clear regulations and effective enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Cities like Shanghai have already implemented bans on loud speakers and videos in their subway system, while France has begun fining passengers were using phone speakers in stations, measures that have shown promising results.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Public buses and trains could be outfitted with basic sound monitoring devices that automatically alert transport staff when noise levels spike significantly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Alternatively, staff and fare inspectors could use portable meters to verify whether a passenger's device is reaching the threshold.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Such technology already exists and its integration will provide evidence-based grounds for issuing warnings or fines.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For example, staff could perform regular checks supported by roving inspector teams that respond to commuter reports via a dedicated mobile app or hotline.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If a train carriage is especially noisy, a commuter could perhaps tap an in-app report noise button.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The station officer at the next stop alerted in real time could board and assess the situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Upon confirming excessive noise, and the officer could issue an immediate warning or a small fine.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: A similar reporting mechanism can be implemented for buses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I favour showing leniency to first-time offenders with a warning or a small fine.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, their identification and details can be recorded to ensure tracking for subsequent offences, which can also lead to higher subsequent fines.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Clear decibel thresholds, empowered enforcement officers, real-time reporting tools and escalating penalty structure and tools for public awareness will help strike the right balance between personal freedom and communal well-being.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, I also read of bus passengers behaving in an inconsiderate manner by putting up their legs on the bus seats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In January 2025, there was a report of two men who were charged for urinating at MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This kind of poor behaviour can make our public transport journey less comfortable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I notice that there are new stickers on MRT trains that tell commuters to “keep the volume low”, “occupy only one seat” and “no sitting on the floor”.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or are they intended to remind commuters on the need to be considerate to other public transport users?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the signs are meant to be enforced, how does LTA determine what level of volume is too loud to be unacceptable and what if a passenger insist on occupying another seat with his bag?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, to fulfil Singapore’s car-lite ambitions, having a world-class public transport system must be a top priority.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This means making it accessible to all, including seniors, children, young parents with prams and wheelchair users, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A safe and pleasant commuter experience helps position public transport as the mode of choice.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As a frequent user of the MRT, this is why I have been asking Parliamentary Questions around this.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, last year, I raised the need to enhance and ensure the consistent display of LCD screens, so that commuters can read the route map and be able to count the stops before their destination at all times.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To reduce the risk of crowd-related collisions, I also suggested wayfinding floor graphics that are immediately visible upon exiting train cabins, guiding commuters towards elevators on MRT platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is often difficult to locate the nearest lift, especially during peak hours, and on crowded platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Even more so when taller commuters obstruct the view of wheelchair users, disrupting their ability to navigate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This complements existing tactile guiding systems, and helps reduce directional ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I had asked about the implementation of gap fillers and ways to further reduce the height difference between the platform and train floor.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This too, is in the interest of safety and independent commuting.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry share if it has any updates on these suggestions or upcoming plans to further enhance the commuter experience?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Ministry periodically collects feedback through platforms like CrowdTaskSG.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A recent example was the study titled, “User Research: Wayfinding on MRT Network” by LTA.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such studies are commendable, as user feedback is the best form of feedback.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, can the Ministry clarify how it ensures the collection of a representative sample, as such online channels may end up excluding less digitally-savvy groups, like our seniors.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could consider dedicated outreaches to seniors and persons with disabilities for a broader and more inclusive engagement.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, public transport may not be feasible for some persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To facilitate participation in education, employment and even play, can the Ministry elaborate if there are future plans to increase the availability and affordability of wheelchair transport?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, road safety is a key priority, especially for our most vulnerable pedestrians, the young, the elderly and those who are physically and visually handicapped.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: While Singapore has made significant progress in reducing road accidents, we must continue strengthening measures to ensure a safer environment for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Can we introduce more senior- and handicap-friendly crossings, such as extended green man timings, pedestrian refuge islands and tactile guides?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Are there plans to expand traffic calming measures in school zones and estates with high elderly population?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Can we explore smart traffic signals that adjust based on pedestrian movement or expand automated enforcement to deter speeding in pedestrian-heavy areas?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Beyond infrastructure, public awareness and enforcement are crucial.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: How can we further educate road users while strengthening measures against reckless driving?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: By improving infrastructure, leveraging on technology and fostering greater awareness, we can create a safer, more inclusive environment for all pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Surely, this is more convenient for all the commuters.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are two neighbourhood centres with each housing a food centre, wet market, shops and supermarket.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These two neighbourhood centres, Blocks 537 to 539 and Blocks 509 to 511 precincts of Bedok North Steet 3, are the focal points for my residents for their daily needs, such as grocery shopping and eating their meals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Like any other neighbourhood centres, they also attract many non-residents to come and shop and fulfil their food cravings when many come by their own vehicles or commute by public transport.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Member of Parliament for Jalan Kayu, I deeply appreciate LTA’s selection to make the streets there more friendly and safe for pedestrians and cyclists as the estate has one of the highest proportions of seniors above 60 years old in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the same note, Seletar Hill, one of four Jalan Kayu private estates, also has one of the highest proportion of seniors above 60 years old in my constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, when is LTA planning to start consultation with resident networks on the selection and design of the Friendly Streets initiative for private estates?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The continued occurrence of incidents, such as the fatal collision between a 20-year-old e-scooter rider and an elderly woman in Bedok North last year, has kept the issue of pathway safety on the public’s consciousness.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I wonder if this provision is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Walking from point-to-point is a daily reality for many of them.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this instance, I propose widening the shared pathway for the duration of the adjacent construction, by temporarily concretising an adjacent grass strip, measuring 0.45 metres in width.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Singapore society ages, and as we evolve how we complete our last-mile commute, I hope our provisions can spare a thought for the safety of the vulnerable ones in our community.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: At the COS debate last year, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that the Government had accepted the Active Mobility Advisory Panel’s recommendations on the use of personal mobility aids.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With our rapidly ageing population, we will observe greater adoption of these vehicles in our estates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will MOT ensure that sellers and users are sufficiently informed of the new regulations?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What measures does MOT have in place to check on and allow only imported devices that meet the regulatory requirements?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Minister share its public education and communication plans on the new regulations for the general public, especially for the PMA users?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the enforcement measures on the ground to ensure that PMA users comply with the new regulations?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will MOT be increasing the recruitment of enforcement officers and tap on technology to deter and identify illegal uses of PMAs?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Residents who have weak limbs find these devices very useful in enabling them to move around independently.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Unfortunately, there are also many irresponsible riders who illegally modify them and use the PMDs or e-bikes to race on the roads and to ride recklessly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This poses a danger to both the rider and to other road users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Some riders may not even know the highway code but they are allowed to race the PMDs on the roads.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In mid-February, it was reported that a group of young people were arrested for riding illegally modified or non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This is probably the tip of the iceberg as I regularly receive many other complaints about such reckless riders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I also received complaints that some of the PMD users would charge their illegally modified PMDs at the HDB void deck and even bring them onto MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This poses a fire risk to the other residents in the block and to other commuters who may be on the train.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Will action be taken against retailers who sell illegally modified PMDs or help to modify the PMAs illegally or if they sell the riders non-compliant batteries?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: These retailers are also complicit in abetting the commission of an offence and I would urge LTA to take action against them and punish them accordingly.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Occupational drivers, such as those driving heavy vehicles, taxis, private-hire and delivery vehicles, could be motivated by incentives or penalties to drive for long hours without breaks.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Thus, employers or platform operators must ensure that such incentive and penalty systems do not increase driver fatigue and compromise vehicular safety.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Could the Ministry share how it is working with stakeholders to reinforce shared responsibility for the safety of occupational drivers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In her recent Parliamentary Question reply, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor highlighted examples of companies already using buses to ferry workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In fact, I have visited many of these companies, sometimes in the wee hours of the morning, and I commend them for their commitment to safer worker transportation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: For specialist tradesmen and small businesses, I urge these companies not to co-mingle people and goods at the back of lorries, as it is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Under the Road Traffic Act, all equipment on board lorries must be properly secured to ensure the safety of all road users and workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I urge LTA and the Traffic Police to step up joint enforcement action against companies which fail to do so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The business landscape has evolved for our P2P drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The introduction of ride hail services and the use of apps for booking of transport have changed Singaporean commuter behaviours, and we see, indeed, that there is a gradual confluence of taxi and PHV business models.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our drivers have told us it is increasingly difficult for driving to be sustainable, given the escalating costs of business which includes petrol prices, rental fees and maintenance costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As we look to rationalising and revitalising our P2P business models – between ride-hail/street-hail, taxi platforms – it is important to note that our drivers have also indicated their growing insecurities with their earnings, welfare and benefits with their platform partners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The lack of transparency when it comes to the distribution of work, price fluctuations and campaigns impact the earnings of our drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some of our drivers say that they find themselves struggling due to hidden costs and unclear earning structures, especially with the introduction of mandatory CPF from platforms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In the review, can the Ministry consider putting in more safeguards to protect the earnings of our drivers, especially since our drivers, unlike the truly self-employed, are subject to the management controls and rules of engagement of their platform partners?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Mr Chairman, in addition, there continues to be demand amongst our seniors, both drivers and commuters, for street-hail services, and there are currently still drivers who are not on any booking apps.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The primary reason given is that they find the current user interface of booking apps complicated and they are not digitally savvy enough to navigate these apps effectively.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Will the Ministry consider the implementation of a simplified community app for seniors who struggle with technology so that they can gently ease themselves into the more convenient world of ride-hailing?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as I run a company that leases out taxis, limousines and private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The taxi industry has been a cornerstone of Singapore’s transport, serving commuters faithfully despite PHC disruptions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Taxis remain vital, especially for street-hail customers like tourists and those who are less familiar with phone apps.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Their lifespan: a PHC can operate beyond 10 years, while taxis cannot.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Last but not least, the regulation: the PHC numbers are unregulated, whereas taxi numbers are capped.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Of these, flexibility stands out as the most critical advantage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It allows PHC drivers to maximise the usage of their vehicles, a significant benefit in Singapore, where car ownership is costly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: To address this imbalance, I propose looking to Montreal in Canada, as an example.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This adjustment would create a more level playing field and help sustain the taxi industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In addition, a fast-charging infrastructure is crucial for electric taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: LTA needs to collaborate with the Energy Market Authority, Singapore Power and other stakeholders to accelerate the fast charger installation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Without this, electric taxis may struggle to support their sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Without intervention, we risk losing a vital service that has long been a pillar of our transport system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Let us work together to preserve the taxi industry for future generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman point-to-point (P2P) services play an important role being a convenient and, at times, essential supplement to our public transport system, by providing direct access to specific locations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Our main P2P providers are taxis and private hire vehicles (PHV).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Although PHVs have been increasing their market share in recent years, taxis continue to have an important role.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Their service supply is more stable and they provide street-hail services welcomed by tourists and those who are less tech-savvy, such as the elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: At locations with high passenger traffic, such as Changi Airport, tourist attractions, shopping malls and hospitals, their availability provides comforting assurance to their users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will the Ministry look into improving passengers’ experiences of all P2P transport services in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Commuting in private hire cars (PHCs) has become an integral part of our local transport mix.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While many Singaporeans have embraced PHCs as a commute modality, the fact that PHCs are not allowed to pick-up and drop-off passengers at taxi stands runs counter to common sense.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Why not allow the use of available infrastructure to facilitate safe pick-up and drop-off for PHC users?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From both the convenience and safety standpoints, doing so makes good sense.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I agree with the need to restrict vehicles other than taxis from stopping or parking, I urge LTA and MOT to reconsider allowing PHCs to pick-up and drop-off passengers at taxi stands and stops.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Taxi drivers and private hire vehicle drivers face higher operating costs arising from payments for vehicle leasing, insurances and more.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Because the trip earnings of these point-to-point drivers fluctuate depending on the platforms' algorithms, drivers are stressed by financial precarity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Platform drivers have asked that platforms disclose what is the average fare per hour or per kilometre.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Such information helps them to determine if they can sustain a viable livelihood as a platform driver.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: This in turn ensures that the Government's moves to uplift platform workers does translate to sustainable point-to-point transport services.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Drivers have also asked that platforms provide clear and timely communication to drivers if changes to platform policies are likely to impact on drivers' earnings and work schedules.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Could the Ministry share its plans to address these concerns?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is thus common for drivers to operate using multiple platforms to ensure a steady stream of passengers and boost their earnings – also known as "multi-homing".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, this must be balanced against the risk that PTP drivers have insufficient rest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Following the passing of the Platform Workers Act 2024, tying drivers to a single or primary platform may be necessary for effective regulation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The high COE price has also been blamed for the increased costs of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Many Singaporeans feel that the high cost of COE was due to excessive demand from the bidders of PHCs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: They feel that many private hire companies buy the cars for hire and then subsequently sell the cars to the hirers for their personal use.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The question is whether these new measures will help manage the increasing costs of the COE.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Will LTA introduce any other measures to manage COE costs like imposing the equivalent of additional duty for the buyers of more than two cars.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Will the introduction of ERP 2.0 allow the injection of more COEs and help reduce COE prices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The existing vehicle quota system of Vehicle Quota System (VQS) maintains COEs that last for 10 years for the first instance and can be renewed for either five- or 10-year periods thereafter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the inception of the VQS, the 10-year duration was chosen because it will align with the existing limit of the preferential additional registration fee or part rebate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although one could argue that back in 1990, they were also broadly aligned with factors driving vehicle turnover, such as safety, efficiency emissions and maintenance costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With new electric vehicles (EVs), however, these factors are likely to be dominated by a wholly different consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is consistent with the practice of designating battery end of life at 70% of the maximum charge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since the cost of replacing a battery outside of the warranty is prohibitively expensive; estimated at around a third of the cost of the actual vehicle, many would consider this an opportune time to replace the car altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can thus regard eight years as a reasonable lower bound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But research suggests that retiring the battery so early, severely under-utilises it and, given the environmental cost of battery manufacture, undermines the EVs sustainability proposition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Industry experts tend to place the equivalent mileage at closer to at least 300 and 20,000 kilometres – double that of the standard warranty distance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even if the battery were changed only once at eight years, it would make sense to stretch out the new battery another eight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, this will afford an equivalent upper bound that amounts to 16 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is much uncertainty over the genuine economic and technical lifespan of an EV.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In light of this, the existing practice of the Ministry, which disallows the repeated renewal of shorter term COEs, should also be eliminated to preserve the maximum flexibility for EV drivers to extend the use of an environmentally friendly car.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The claim that returning short-term COEs into the bidding pool preserves equity between existing and prospective owners of cars, has never made much sense to me, since it applies with equal force to longer-term COEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But insisting on this practice makes even less sense for vehicles that will otherwise endure even longer than the typical internal combustion engine (ICE) equivalents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For those who desire a shorter term for renewals, much like the present five-year COE, and eight-year duration will also coincide with one battery lifecycle.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, today, there is greater awareness amongst Singaporeans about electrical vehicles.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) has made the availability of EV charging stations as accessible as possible in many parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the Enhanced Vehicular Emissions Scheme (VES) provides rebates for vehicles with lower emissions, further incentivising the adoption of cleaner energy vehicles.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, Sir, I have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: First, could the Ministry consider Enhanced Financial Incentives in the form of increase in subsidies or rebates to reduce the initial purchase cost of EVs, making them more accessible to a broader segment of the population.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The decarbonisation of heavy vehicles is a critical issue which the MOT has been grappling with for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is an undeniable fact that heavy vehicles, including trucks, buses and freight carriers contribute significantly to the carbon emissions in our transport sector.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The MOT must take a proactive stance in implementing measures to decarbonise heavy vehicles, not just for the sake of compliance, but to actively combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOT also consider incentivising industries to adopt these green technologies by offering subsidies or tax relief, making it cost-effective for businesses to transition?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, what efforts has the Ministry undertaken so far, to engage with stakeholders in the logistics and transportation sectors, ensuring that these policies align with their operational needs?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will resume at 3.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.54 pm until 3.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Before I proceed further, I forgot to mention, I declare my interest as the advisor to Singapore's Transport Association.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What is the current state of the electrification of our heavy vehicles?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Besides the Heavy Vehicle Zero Emissions Scheme and Electric Heavy Vehicle Charger Grant announced by Prime Minister in Budget 2025, we will need to do more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As our EV Road Map sets out, vehicle taxes and incentives should be complemented by regulations and standards, EV charger deployment and industry partnerships.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To improve charger availability for heavy vehicles, is it possible to explore the possibility of centralised heavy vehicle chargers at centralised parking facilities for heavy vehicles that would complement chargers installed within vehicle owners' premises?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: With rising EV adoptions, will there be sufficient EV chargers across Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Beyond LTA's current plan to install chargers at HDB car parks, is LTA prepared to incentivise the private sector to install more chargers, including fast chargers, at commercial buildings and private residential residences?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In addition, how is EV adoption progressing for commercial vehicles, particularly heavy vehicles?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Will LTA introduce more incentives to encourage EV adoption in this sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Vehicle owner awareness and even inertia may play a role too.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the steps that will be taken to incentivise businesses to opt for environmentally friendlier options for commercial vehicles, especially heavy vehicles?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Has the Ministry engaged the owners of commercial vehicles about the adoption of greener vehicles and, if so, what are their feedback and main concerns?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will MOT capitalise on this growth and develop our passenger markets, in particular, the top five: China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Australia and Thailand?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are MOT's plans to maintain Singapore as an air hub in the face of growing competition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our cargo hub also enjoyed exciting growth last year, across exports, imports and transshipments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the Ministry's plans to boost our capacity for cargo handling, in terms of our infrastructure, processes, manpower and technology development?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Ministry share its programmes to catalyse the development of our air hub and cargo hub in the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: More international shipping groups and maritime-related companies have been set up or expanded their operations here.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: To maintain our lead and market share, even as we are going through the green transition and fending off cybersecurity threats to our maritime operations, we need to continue to innovate and automate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Much of these developments hinge upon attracting and retaining the right talent and workforce development.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: This industry faces manpower challenges due to physically strenuous roles and demanding working environment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the innovations and infrastructure enhancements that are being implemented to help improve efficiency and reduce manpower needs?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mark Lee, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To stay ahead, we must continue to enhance our infrastructure, leverage technology, and strengthen our trade and logistics ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Ministry ensuring that Singapore remains the preferred hub for global supply chains, particularly as regional players ramp up their capabilities?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What measures are in place to enhance port and airport efficiency, integrate smart logistics solutions and deepen trade connectivity?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As businesses seek resilient and cost-effective supply chain solutions, how can we further strengthen partnerships, improve multimodal connectivity and attract more high-value logistics activities to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As global aviation becomes increasingly competitive, Singapore must continue to leverage technology to enhance productivity, support workers and maintain our position as a premium aviation hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With advancements like AI-driven security screening and Terminal 5 on the horizon, how will the Ministry drive wider industry adoption of automation, digitalisation and AI to enhance efficiency and keep costs competitive?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond infrastructure, how can the Ministry support airlines, logistics providers and aviation services in investing in emerging technologies to stay ahead of regional competition?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond infrastructure, how will the Ministry support the wider aviation sector, including airlines, logistics providers and support services, in investing in emerging technologies to stay ahead of regional competition?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given that other air hubs are rapidly upgrading, how can Singapore ensure continuous innovation and workforce upskilling to reinforce our status as a global leader in aviation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To stay ahead of rapidly improving regional airports, we must boost productivity, enhance connectivity and strengthen our position as a key business and travel destination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the airport, the broader air hub ecosystem must also grow in tandem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Critical industries, such as aerospace, maintenance, repair and operations (MRO), logistics supply chain and airside services, need a coordinated strategy that aligns infrastructure expansion, workforce readiness, sustainability, supply chain resilience and industry development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Collaboration among key players, Singapore Airlines, Changi Airport Group, Singapore Tourism Board and the hospitality sector, just to name some, must also be deepened to enhance Singapore's Air Hub value proposition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Dubai offers a strong model where its airline, tourism board and airport operator work in synergy to position the city as a premier travel destination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As Changi Airport expands, how can we optimise urban planning and resource allocation in areas, such as Loyang Industrial Estate, Changi Business Park, Pasir Ris, Punggol Digital District and Seletar, to reinforce growth and strengthen our aviation sector?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the Government's long-term roadmap to integrate these elements and ensure Singapore's Air Hub's competitiveness into the future?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In an increasingly competitive global landscape, it is critical that Singapore continues to build on its relevancy as an international hub for business and trade.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: At the heart of the matter, we need to ensure that our workforce is given the opportunity to upskill and that there are clearly articulated career progression pathways for our workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Can the Ministry provide us with an update on the Tuas Port Developments and how can Singapore prepare our employees for a progressive maritime career, while smoothening the process for professionals making mid-career switches?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Barely two to six years ago, stagnating container traffic suggested that Singapore may have reached its hub potential as competition from nearby ports, like Tanjung Pelepas grew.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Emerging ports, such as those in Ho Chi Minh and Hai Phong in Vietnam or Tanjung Priok in Jakarta, are rapidly improving their port infrastructure and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This has been reflected by the increasing scores of ports in Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia on the United Nations Trade and Development's (UNCTAD's) Port Connectivity Index.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In addition to being an international maritime centre, Singapore is the top bunkering port and busiest container transshipment hub in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: To keep Singapore's lead in this sector, we need to continuously improve the standard and range of services by tapping on new technologies and refine processes to facilitate greater efficiency, consistency and reliability of our maritime services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: At the core of all these are our people whose dedication, expertise, skills and hard work have enabled our maritime centre and port to perform outstandingly year after year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are MOT's plans for our maritime workforce's development to elevate their competencies and boost their productivities?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How would the Ministry support the adoptions of new technologies to improve existing processes and increase the overall productivity of the maritime sector?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Neil Parekh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The foundation of our success lies in one crucial element: our people.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The right skills and expertise are essential to maintaining the competitiveness of our international maritime centre and hub port.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The maritime industry is dynamic and fast evolving, demanding a workforce that is not only highly skilled, but also adaptable to new technologies and global trends.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As the maritime industry embarks on its sustainability transformation, the safety of alternative fuels remains a critical concern.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As a global maritime hub, Singapore is fully committed to leading this transition while ensuring the highest safety standards.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Is qualified manpower available to meet the challenges facing the maritime industry in alternative fuels?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the past 60 years of Singapore's nation-building journey, we worked hard as one people to overcome our challenges and turned them into opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We developed our communications and transport infrastructure and built Singapore as a global transport hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This remains a key growth strategy, one which strengthens our supply-chain resilience, our connections to the world and our geostrategic relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We equipped our companies and workers to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, our homegrown companies, such as PSA, Changi Airport Group, Singapore Airlines and SATS are global leaders, bringing Singapore to the world and the world to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Equally important was how we connected Singaporeans to people and places at home through national projects, such as the MRT system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat noted, transportation has played a vital role in our nation's development and will continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At this year's COS, we will build on our strengths to improve the way we live, move, and connect through three areas: first, stronger connectivity; second, safer and more comfortable journeys; third, more opportunities for businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our MRT system opened on 7 November 1987 with five stations – Yio Chu Kang, Ang Mo Kio, Bishan, Braddell and Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From these early foundations, the network has grown significantly, with the North-East Line in 2003, Circle Line in 2009, Downtown Line in 2013 and Thomson-East Coast Line in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will add new stations or lines every year till the end of this decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A few days ago, we opened Hume station on the Downtown Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Between 2027 and 2029, we will open parts of the Jurong Region Line, starting with Choa Chu Kang to Boon Lay and Tawas, followed by Tengah to Pandan Reservoir, and eventually connecting to NTU Campus and Jurong Pier.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From 2030, we will progressively open our eighth MRT Line, the Cross Island Line, to connect the eastern, western and northeastern regions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They require careful planning, taking into consideration current and future land-use needs, engineering feasibility and potential environment impact.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also requires political stability, as well as a strong government which can plan long-term, and have the ability and resources to turn these plans into reality, because the plans will span multiple terms of government.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In economies that face persistent budget deficits, they would not have the fiscal resources to implement such long-term large-scale projects.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Several Members, such as Mr Ang Wei Neng, Ms Foo Mee Har, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Leong Mun Wai had previously asked about rail connectivity in the western region.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Last year, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor and I provided updates on one of the projects which LTA has been studying – the West Coast Extension (WCE).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will enhance rail connectivity for residents in the West, and support future developments along the corridor.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will reduce journey times to the city centre by up to 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The WCE will also enhance the overall resilience of our rail network, by providing an alternative via the Cross Island Line, and to the city centre via Circle Line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Ong Hua Han asked about a new rail line to serve residents in the north and northeast regions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When the Land Transport Master Plan (LTMP) 2040 was released in 2019, we had shared plans for feasibility studies into a new line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This line, tentatively called the Seletar Line, could serve areas, such as Woodlands, Sembawang, Sengkang West, Serangoon North, Whampoa, Kallang, and the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I hope it could also go through some parts of Toa Payoh!

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also identified another corridor for a new rail line, tentatively called the Tengah Line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Similarly, feasibility studies are ongoing to assess if such a line could supplement the transport network in the west and northwest regions, serving areas, such as Tengah, Bukit Batok, Queensway and Bukit Merah.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Based on LTA's preliminary assessments, these two potential rail lines could meet at the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our feasibility studies will therefore look into the possibility of linking the two lines into a single line, for more seamless connectivity and better efficiency for commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will benefit more than 400,000 households who will be within a 10-minute walk from this new combined line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For our MRT system to remain the backbone of our public transport network, our efforts must go beyond growing the rail network, to ensuring that trains continue to operate safely and reliably for all commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a challenging task, as our MRT network is an expanding system with many inter-connected elements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The rail network relies on the dedication of 7,000 workers and the commitment of tripartite partners to operate smoothly every day.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the past decade, we have invested heavily and made significant strides in rail reliability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We set ourselves a high bar – to achieve one million mean kilometres between failure, or MKBF, and have consistently achieved this since 2019.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MKBF is a reliability benchmark used by many metros globally, and the one million MKBF benchmark puts us among the top performing metros in the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Since 2020, the Government has supported operators to improve maintenance and operation standards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also supported rail sector workers to strengthen their capabilities and improve productivity, through training grants and productivity incentives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Maintaining high standards will become more challenging as our network grows.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have one of the densest networks in the world and with more trains covering longer distances, sustaining a high reliability target of one million MKBF will require even greater effort.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is also a need to manage both newer and older systems and assets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will enhance the way we monitor and maintain our assets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The additional funding will also support skills upgrading for our workers to keep pace with these developments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This move builds on the New Rail Financing Framework (NRFF), where LTA handles asset procurement and replacement, and the operators handle asset maintenance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Under this framework, LTA holds our operators accountable for their maintenance of assets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also have incentives and performance standards in place to ensure that operators deliver good, reliable service.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If any operator does not perform, it could face financial penalties and miss out on incentives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This approach has helped us to improve reliability and achieve good outcomes for commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As more of our rail assets approach the end of their service life, we will need to invest more to improve life cycle management so that we optimise the lifespan of our assets while making replacements in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The enhanced NRFF will allow us to: expand condition monitoring capabilities for more proactive intervention and targeted maintenance; carry out targeted replacements of sub-systems and components to better sustain the useful life of our assets; and scale up the adoption of new technologies to boost maintenance efficiency and effectiveness across the sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our operators will continue to be responsible for the maintenance of assets, as per their existing responsibilities under the NRFF.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With the additional investments, LTA can better optimise the life cycle management of rail assets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will enable LTA and the operators to achieve high reliability standards while keeping a tight control on maintenance and asset replacement costs, which will benefit commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond technology and hardware, we will also invest in uplifting the maintenance capabilities of our entire rail sector and enable tripartite partners – LTA, operators, and workers – to achieve higher levels of safety, reliability and resilience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will strengthen training programmes, provide more opportunities and incentives for workers to upgrade their skills and support rail operators to drive workforce and operations transformation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also continue to learn from leading overseas metros and international rail experts to help us stay at the forefront of rail excellence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over time, as workers upgrade their skills through upskilling and reskilling, they will be able to take on higher value jobs, improve their productivity and earn higher wages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will also help to further uplift standards across the industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we deploy more buses, we will also give them priority on more roads to facilitate their movement and improve their reliability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will provide an update on how we will improve the stability of supply, strengthen contestability and improve passenger experience and access.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Commuters remain at the heart of how we design our transport services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA has been progressively enhancing its infrastructure, working closely with Grassroots Advisers and community leaders to better serve our commuters and residents in different towns across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The design for MRT stations and bus interchanges has evolved and improved over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, newer train stations and bus interchanges, such as Punggol Coast station on the North-East Line and Buangkok Bus Interchange, are better integrated with residential and commercial developments, making them more accessible and vibrant.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our stations, interchanges, trains and buses have also been equipped with more features to improve accessibility for passengers of diverse needs, such as family-friendly facilities and wheelchair-friendly Passenger Service Centres.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA has developed strong engineering expertise to build our large-scale infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to complement this by enhancing LTA’s capabilities to integrate human-centric design with its engineering expertise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
