text: Just like how companies like Apple and Dyson are known for combining engineering with design to bring greater value to consumers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to learn from such industry leaders and see how we can make key public transport nodes like MRT stations and bus interchanges more user-friendly, more comfortable and more convenient.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA is planning a multi-year effort to review and improve our infrastructure and services, guided by four "E"s.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will improve the design of all our transport nodes, to apply what we learnt from building new lines, stations and interchanges to enhance our existing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will enlarge the reach and coverage of our commuter infrastructure through features, such as covered linkways, more benches and additional escalators and lifts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will also make it safer and more convenient for our seniors to age well in the community.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our transport nodes can host more community activities, offer better retail and F&B services, and serve as venues for promoting the arts, heritage and music to support our local artists and performers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Commuters can make better use of our spaces and services, through improved signages, wayfinding and digital services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I would like to thank Mr Ong Hua Han for his feedback and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MOT and LTA are committed to making these improvements by learning from best practices, here and abroad.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As the North-South and East-West Lines have been in operation for over 30 years, I asked LTA to look into a multi-year programme to rejuvenate the stations on these lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will study how we can do this through a Station Rejuvenation Programme for the North-South and East-West lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will review the upgrades required for each station, tailored to the station’s ridership, footprint, typology and surrounding developments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will provide more details.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This Station Rejuvenation Programme will refresh our stations, making them more welcoming and user-friendly while preserving key heritage elements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Similarly, our bus interchanges have also grown into familiar community hubs for residents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will open new bus interchanges to provide more convenient transfers and refresh existing ones to improve commuter experience and comfort.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Works have already started at Toa Payoh bus interchange, Singapore’s first integrated transport hub.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In response to Mr Ang Wei Neng, commuters at Bishan, Bukit Merah, Eunos and Tampines bus interchanges can look forward to upgrades with new rain screens, additional benches and fans to improve their comfort and commuting experience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also welcome suggestions and ideas from commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I am glad that Members agree with the Government’s vision to build a car-lite society, where Walk-Cycle-Ride are the main modes of transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA will set aside an experimentation fund to support ideas from commuters and work with them to jointly develop cost-effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While the vast majority of commuters are considerate and gracious, we need to protect the quality of their commute from the small minority of black sheep whose anti-social behaviours and actions cause discomfort and, sometimes, even endanger others.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue with our public education efforts, but we know education alone will not be enough and needs to go together with effective enforcement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I have asked LTA and the operators to step up their Enforcement – which is the fifth "E" – by strengthening our regulatory powers and increasing the penalties to deter egregious commuters, especially repeat offenders and those who refuse to cooperate when they are advised by public transport workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Another key aspect of commuter experience is safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In July last year, we launched the Bus Safety Tripartite Taskforce.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Minister of State Murali Pillai and our tripartite partners sought views from thousands of commuters, bus captains and both local and international safety experts, who shared their ideas to improve safety practices for the public bus sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The task force has submitted its recommendations, which I have accepted.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These include how we can equip buses with more safety features, facilitate their smooth travel on the road, and better support Bus Captains to provide safe journeys for all.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Making roads safer for everyone also means that more pedestrians and cyclists can benefit from active mobility through Friendly Streets and Road Repurposing Projects.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will elaborate on this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While we need to be inclusive to those with genuine mobility needs, we must also ensure the safety of other path users.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will give an update on the implementation timelines for the changes to the safety rules for Personal Mobility Aids that were announced last year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Upon completion, the West Coast extension will reduce commuting time for residents in the West to the city centre.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Additionally, we are exploring the construction of two new MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The first is tentatively named as the Seletar Line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will connect the north and northeast regions to the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The other new MRT line is tentatively named as the Tengah Line, will connect the north and northwest regions to the Greater Southern Waterfront.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If these two MRT lines are feasible, they can be joined to form a longer MRT line – the Seletar-Tengah Line, running from the North to the West through the city centre.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our bus services complement the MRT network in improving the residents' commuting convenience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To date, we have launched 10 new bus routes and enhanced 36 existing bus routes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to improve the designs of MRT stations and bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This year, we plan to rejuvenate the stations on North-South line and East-West line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Furthermore, we are pushing forward with upgrading of bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the coming months, we will open three integrated air-conditioned interchanges at Woodleigh, Pasir Ris, and Punggol Coast.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA also plans to upgrade several bus interchanges which have been in operation for some time, including Toa Payoh and Bishan bus interchanges. : Madam, let me turn to my final topic of how we are providing more opportunities for businesses and workers in the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This Government believes in the importance of planning long term and having the ability and resources to implement our plans effectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is how we developed Singapore into a global aviation and maritime hub, and why we have made significant investments in developing Changi Airport Terminal 5 and Tuas Port.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These achievements do not happen automatically and we should never take our hub status and competitive advantages for granted, given the intense global competition.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singapore remains a leading maritime hub, achieving new records in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to build on this momentum to strengthen our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Minister of State Murali Pillai will provide more details.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The air hub is off to a good start in 2025, with Changi’s passenger numbers exceeding 11.5 million for the first two months of 2025, a 7% increase compared to the same period last year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We added 11 new city links in 2024, to places like Brussels, Guiyang, Phu Quoc and Vancouver.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our strong performance would not have been possible without the collective efforts of the aviation community.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Global passenger volumes are expected to double in the next two decades, with the Asia Pacific regions driving half of this growth.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: T5 will also enhance our hub status and provide new and exciting employment opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As a member state of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and International Maritime Organization (IMO), Singapore is committed to contributing towards ICAO and IMO’s global ambition of achieving net-zero targets by or around 2050.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The United Nations Framework Convention of Climate Change sets the global reporting requirements for greenhouse gas inventories.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Emissions from international aviation and maritime do not accrue to national greenhouse gas inventories.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Likewise, there is no benefit for Changi to move too far ahead of other airports when it comes to adoption of sustainable aviation fuel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: At last year’s COS debate, I explained why we will start with a 1% target in 2026 to spur investments in sustainable aviation fuel production capacity and increase this over time to 3% to 5% by 2030, subject to global developments and the wider availability and adoption of sustainable aviation fuel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I believe this is a pragmatic approach, because the cost of sustainable aviation fuel is currently much higher than conventional jet fuel, and we need to strike a balance between sustainability and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Several countries, including India, Indonesia and the Republic of Korea, have also adopted a 1% initial target before ramping up in subsequent years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The UK started with a 2% sustainable aviation fuel mandate in 2025 and not 10%, as what Mr Tan said.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our approach is to enable our aviation sector to grow and improve environmental sustainability concurrently.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We launched the Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint last year, which sets out Singapore’s medium and long-term goals for international and domestic emissions, and our plans to achieve them with stakeholders across the airport, airline and air traffic management domains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our air hub is a source of many good jobs for Singaporeans and a key enabler for many other sectors in our economy, such as manufacturing, professional services and tourism.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope Mr Dennis Tan is not suggesting that we should forgo building T5, as that would bring more flights to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: How is that good for Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This Government cares about environmental sustainability, but we also care about the well-being of our people, our workers and our businesses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean said, we are climate realists, not climate zealots.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While our air hub is well-placed to ride the winds of growth, competition is intensifying.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are mindful about rising costs faced by aviation stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government is committed to working with the aviation industry to improve our service levels, raise productivity and reduce operating costs where possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we achieve cost savings, we will share these with our industry partners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One of the biggest advantages that Singapore has today over many competitors is our ability to work as one aviation ecosystem and the close tripartite relationship between companies, unions and the Government.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We must continue to leverage on this as we look at ways to enhance Changi’s air hub competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To Mr Mark Lee, Ms Poh Li San and Mr Sharael Taha’s questions, we will strengthen our support for Changi in four key areas: Connectivity, Infrastructure, Innovation and Technology, and Manpower.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is on top of the $5 billion top-up to the Changi Airport Development Fund that the Prime Minister announced.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the next few months, CAAS will work with companies and union leaders, Government agencies and international partners to develop schemes in each of these areas that will help our companies and workers to thrive and succeed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: CAAS will work with economic agencies and industry to identify key links and to develop schemes that can accelerate these new connections.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: CAAS will work with aviation stakeholders to plan enabling infrastructure for the Singapore air hub and to coordinate development across companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will provide funding support to accelerate the development of common use infrastructure that will benefit all airport users, to support state-of-the-art, efficient and cost-effective airport operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The technology roadmap will leverage the development of T5 to set up living labs that can be used to testbed and grow new capabilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Skilled manpower is a key competitive factor for air hubs around the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: CAAS will work with aviation companies and unions to grow a quality workforce, comprising a strong Singapore Core complemented by foreign workers who are important contributors to Changi’s overall competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will invest in skills upgrading for our workers and redesign jobs to better attract and retain local workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In this way, our air hub can continue to remain competitive and provide good employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will strengthen Changi’s position as a trusted, efficient and well-connected air cargo hub.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will be complemented by the Airport Logistics Park 2 that was announced last year, which will also provide additional capacity to anchor logistics activities, including Regional Distribution Centres and freight forwarding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the lead-up to these developments, we will continue to work with industry partners to ensure we have sufficient capacity to meet growing air cargo demand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a good example of how we work together as a One Aviation Community, to support one another and, ultimately, to enhance Changi’s competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will harness technology to uplift productivity and allow our cargo workers to optimise their time and resources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: CAAS and Changi Airport Group are supporting the air cargo community to implement an ecosystem digital solution for truck dock slot pre-booking, with full roll-out expected later this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This transforms cargo collection and lodgement from a “first-come-first-served” basis, to one that is pre-planned and better optimised.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope this can be scaled up and we can reap more benefits.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Transport has played a vital role in this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We built up major transport infrastructure, such as our MRT network, our airport, our seaports, and these have catalysed and enabled the progress of our nation from third-world to first.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we navigate through unchartered waters in an increasingly fragmented and volatile world, the key values from our transport journey remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singapore must continue to stay open and strengthen our connections with the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will always place Singaporeans at the heart of all we do and work with tripartite partners to strengthen our social compact and grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And finally, we will take calculated risks and make bold long-term decisions, as we venture out of our comfort zone to seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, let me share how we will create more friendly and safe journeys, strengthen connectivity in our land transport system and enable businesses to decarbonise their vehicle fleet for a more liveable and sustainable city.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At last year’s COS debate, I announced that Friendly Streets would be expanded to all towns by 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have since completed works for the five Friendly Streets pilots.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also completed engagements and progressively started infrastructure works for the 10 Friendly Streets sites announced last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These locations have a higher proportion of seniors or young families living in public and private housing estates who will benefit most from the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to identify more areas suitable to implement Friendly Streets, possibly Seletar Hills estate, as suggested by Ms Ng Ling Ling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One of the key features of all Friendly Streets is the emphasis on pedestrian safety, as highlighted by Mr Shawn Huang.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That is why Friendly Streets have road humps and narrower road lanes to slow down speeds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Speed limits are also lowered to 40 kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To further enhance pedestrian safety, we will roll out the following initiatives from 1 January 2026.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We made this change because school schedules are increasingly more varied and extends beyond the conventional dismissal times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked agencies to step up enforcement against companies which do not properly secure equipment on board lorries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Agencies will continue to take firm action to enforce this requirement under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It is the responsibility of companies to comply for the safety of their workers and other road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In tandem with Friendly Streets, we are pressing on with our road repurposing projects, with six completed thus far.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Centre dividers and road humps will be added to slow down vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These enhancements will bring about a safer and more comfortable walking and cycling experience between Tanjong Pagar and Maxwell MRT stations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also embark on two new road repurposing projects at Tampines and Bedok.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In Tampines, we observed very high footfall across Tampines Central 5, where around 60,000 pedestrians a day travel between Tampines MRT station and the malls in Tampines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To enhance the commuting experience, we will pedestrianise a 50-metre-long stretch of Tampines Central 5, where commuters can look forward to a seamless walking path between the transport facilities and malls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In Bedok, in collaboration with adviser Cheryl Chan, we will pedestrianise a 90-metre-long stretch of Bedok North Street 4 and close an adjacent HDB car park to create a new community space for residents to come together, and a more comfortable walking experience to and from Bedok 85 Market and Fengshan neighbourhood centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Separately, also in Bedok, Mr Faisal Abdul Manap would be pleased to know that as part of HDB’s upcoming Bedok North Springs BTO, HDB plans to build a high covered linkway across Bedok North Street 3 to Block 509.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Next, Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked for an update on the point-to-point (P2P) transport industry review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Since PHCs entered the sector in 2013, commuters have benefited from a more responsive P2P supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Even so, taxis remain important for meeting P2P demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, as dedicated P2P vehicles, taxis provide a more stable source of supply throughout the day compared to PHCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One-shift taxis spend a median of 49 active hours per week serving P2P trips, compared to 34 by PHCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, taxis can offer street-hail services, which remain important for commuters who may be less familiar with local ride-hail apps, and at locations with very high demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At last year’s COS debate, we converged some regulations between PHCs and taxis to make taxis more viable, as they incur higher operating costs due to existing regulatory differences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, as Mr Ang Wei Neng pointed out, there are still some gaps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This year, we will introduce further changes to the regulatory regime for taxis and PHCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We first suspended the cap in 2021 to help taxi operators replenish their fleet to pre-pandemic numbers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This extended suspension will facilitate the replacement and growth of the taxi fleet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, we will allow taxi operators to convert used vehicles that are less than five years old to taxis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Instead of just buying new vehicles, taxi operators will have an additional option to grow their fleet, which may help to reduce costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will give taxi operators flexibility to resell under-utilised taxis and reduce carrying costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This added flexibility can also reduce operators’ risks when trialling new taxi models, such as bigger, more expensive multipurpose vehicles which can better serve larger families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These moves give taxi operators more flexibility to manage cost and grow their fleet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It also helps to stabilise the PHC supply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Every day, four million trips are made on our public buses by commuters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: At the peak, about 6,000 public buses ply our roads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: A system at this scale, which includes almost 10,000 bus captains, requires a sustained and unceasing effort to maintain a strong safety record.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Government, together with our tripartite partners, are fully committed to this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But to succeed, we need the public behind us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As part of this effort, the Bus Safety Tripartite Taskforce was formed in July last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The task force approached this exercise in the spirit of ensuring that commuters, bus captains and other road users continue to have strong confidence in the safety of our public buses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We would like to thank all stakeholders who participated in this important work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are starting from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The annual number of serious road accidents involving public buses has been stable in the past few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Members of the public gave feedback on bus captains' driving, the design of buses, as well as bus scheduling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In addition, they shared real life challenges faced while on the road – motorists encroaching into bus priority boxes, or yellow boxes and bus lanes, as well as with cyclists who cycle close to the blind spots of the buses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The task force has taken a serious look at all these suggestions and consulted with both local and international safety practitioners and experts from the bus sector, before arriving at its recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Shawn Huang asked how we can better support bus captains in carrying out their role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Indeed, a common thread throughout the task force's discussion is that bus captains have a demanding job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In my first meeting with public transport union leaders after we formed this task force, Brother Peh Chee Kang, Vice President of the National Transport Workers' Union, pointed out that driving a public bus is like piloting an aircraft.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Besides operating large vehicles through busy streets while staying on schedule, bus captains must also take care of the safety of passengers and help commuters navigate to their destination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Unlike planes, there is no autopilot available for our bus captains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: They are constantly multitasking and looking out for other road users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The task force was clear that ensuring bus safety means giving our bus captains the best support to do their job well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our recommendations were focused on two major aspects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, equipping bus captains with the right tools; and second, providing them with a conducive working environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Today, I will highlight a few key recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The first area is technologies to improve the situational awareness of our bus captains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Bus Captain Mohammed Syazwan Bin Mohammed Salim from Tower Transit Singapore is one of those who experienced first-hand how anti-fatigue systems can enhance road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The system actively prompted him when he yawned, which was useful in maintaining his alertness while driving and ensured the safety of the bus captain as well as commuters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, technology helps our commuters and other road users stay safe when they are on or around buses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In this regard, the task force recommended a number of safety features, such as better torque management, audio safety announcements onboard buses and an enhanced rear electronic display system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To address the feedback by bus captains on having to multi-task, LTA will also explore whether the number of display units in the driving cabin can be reduced to lessen the cognitive load on bus captains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked how we can further improve the working conditions of bus captains to help manage their workload.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This brings us to the other major set of recommendations by the task force that deals with the human dimension of safety, focused on creating a more conducive working environment for bus captains to perform their roles effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We have a range of recommendations in this area, and I will focus on bus runtimes and training for bus captains, which we believe will have the broadest impact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The runtime is the total time taken for a bus captain to complete a route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It affects safety because if runtimes are not scheduled correctly, bus captains come under pressure to stay on schedule.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Today, bus operators, bus captains, together with LTA, already do regular reviews of runtimes to account for changes in traffic conditions and travel patterns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But beyond having realistic runtimes, the task force felt that runtimes should not be too long.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As Mr Ang Wei Neng pointed out, we have some routes with scheduled runtimes exceeding two hours, and bus captains gave feedback that such prolonged periods of continuous driving can cause discomfort for them, such as the need for toilet breaks, and could cause lapses in concentration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In addition, LTA and bus operators will review our existing bus services with long runtimes, to see how we can make them more manageable for our bus captains, such as by adjusting the routes or swapping bus captains in the middle of a long route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As any adjustments will have an impact on commuters, we will review such routes carefully and implement any changes progressively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Besides scheduling, the task force made a number of recommendations on bus captain training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In our engagements, the task force observed different models, both locally and abroad, of how a strong training regime can make a difference to driver confidence and retention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Under this system, bus operators will track the number of training points that their bus captains obtain per year, corresponding to a baseline level of continuing training each year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This ensures that all bus captains receive the necessary training to refresh their skills and keep up to date with best practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On the Government's part, the Singapore Bus Academy will improve its training offerings, to better support bus operators and bus captains to achieve their training targets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will share more details on these in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Besides improving the working conditions for our bus captains, Mr Saktiandi will be glad to note that the task force has also made several recommendations to improve the road environment to better support bus operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: One aspect that affects all road users is the management of road works.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Bus captains told us that they encounter situations where barriers are placed improperly, resulting in difficulty faced in manoeuvring buses through affected stretches, or when inexperienced road marshals do not provide proper guidance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To address this issue, LTA will work with relevant agencies to upskill workers responsible for managing traffic during road works, to make sure that contractors are able to comply with regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will also review the penalty framework, to take a tougher stance against contractors who do not comply and cause obstructions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: LTA and the bus operators will continue to work with organisations, such as Traffic Police and the Singapore Road Safety Council, to carry out publicity efforts to improve commuters' awareness of safe practices onboard buses, as well as other road users' awareness of and compliance with measures to facilitate bus movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will provide more details on how we will be implementing these and other recommendations of the task force in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As Minister Chee mentioned, Maritime Singapore did well last year, breaking several records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The International Maritime Centre grew in scale and diversity, too, with close to 200 shipping groups with a presence in Singapore and more than 30 companies were established or expanded operations here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we achieved these records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: While other ports in countries with more land and labour can compete on cost and larger consumption bases, Singapore competes on efficiency and reliability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Due to the Red Sea crisis and congestion in ports around the world, shipping lines relied on Singapore to handle increasingly complex cargo movements and demand as they unloaded cargoes bound for Asian ports beyond Singapore and used Singapore to rearrange containers on vessels to mitigate delays.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Through these challenges, we remained resilient, thanks to our tripartite partners and the hard work of our maritime workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With strong competition and an uncertain outlook ahead, we cannot rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Because of our stable political environment, we are able to plan and build for the future with the multi-decade development of Tuas Port.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: When completed in the 2040s, Tuas Port will have more than 60 berths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As Prime Minister Wong said in his Budget speech, global economic competition is intensifying and we will be left behind if we fail to stay competitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked how we will ensure that we remain competitive amidst fierce competition in the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We plan to seize opportunities amidst future growth and challenges in three areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, technology; second. decarbonisation; and third, talent development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On technology, we are leveraging technology to sharpen Maritime Singapore's competitive edge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Poh Li San's questions, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) will use technology to streamline port and marine services to enable the industry to enjoy higher productivity and reduced costs and manpower needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: One example is the use of AI to streamline the processing of Port Clearance Certificates by reducing the need to manually input information from multiple ship certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This system will be implemented over the next few years and enhance the accuracy of data entry and verification, and reduce the time taken to obtain the Certificate from up to three days to just a few minutes!

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MPA is on track to complete the third and final phase of Maritime 5G coverage by this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Stronger connectivity, more consistent data coverage and bandwidth will enable the provision of new maritime services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Together, this means that successful pilots for innovative solutions will more quickly become a part of day-to-day port operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will also develop response capabilities using drones to track and enhance safety for first responders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Next, we will position ourselves as a bunkering hub for alternative fuels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Building on our hard-earned reputation as a reliable bunkering hub, we are committed to support the industry's safe transition to alternative fuels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are upgrading the provisional national quality standard for marine biofuel into a Technical Reference to include biofuel blends up to 100% biofuel and non-FAME products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This complements the International Maritime Organization's recent announcement that conventional oil tankers may soon be allowed to carry biofuel blends containing up to 30% biofuel, instead of the current limit of 25% biofuel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MPA and Enterprise Singapore will launch a standard on the requirements for methanol bunkering and MPA will launch standards on the equipment and operational efficiency for methanol bunker tankers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This marks an important step towards operationalising methanol bunkering at scale in our port.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are also targeting to launch a new standard for ammonia bunkering this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Neil Parekh and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked how we can ensure that we have a robust pipeline of talent with the right skills and competencies to maintain the competitiveness and productivity of Maritime Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MPA will also support the onboarding of MLP alumni to the Singapore Leaders' Network, a leadership community that prepares Singaporeans for regional and global leadership roles by providing overseas transition support and mentorship opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Together, these changes will strengthen cross-sector collaboration and provide opportunities for maritime professionals to learn about adjacent sectors and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, we are equipping workers with new skills to better meet industry needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MPA has established the Maritime Energy Training Facility to train the global maritime workforce in safe handling and operating of vessels using alternative fuels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: MPA is also on track to launch the Maritime Testbed of Shipboard Operational Technology System (MariOT) by March 2025, which provides training in cybersecurity for operational technology systems in a realistic shipboard environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Over the next three years, we expect more than 300 students and professionals to benefit from this simulation platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Working with our partners, we will continue to invest in a strong pipeline of talent to the maritime industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: On both land and sea, you will see that it is our people that makes the difference and this Government will continue to invest in this critical human dimension, for now and into the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Chairman, allow me to share how we are making journeys on public paths and public transport safer and more comfortable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, as announced last year, we will implement new rules to curb the misuse of Personal Mobility Aids (PMAs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we will improve the commuting experience on public transport, by rejuvenating our stations and cultivating a better commuting culture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Last year, the Government accepted the Active Mobility Advisory Panel's (AMAP's) recommendations to tighten regulations for PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have observed more able-bodied individuals misusing PMAs, which are meant for those with mobility needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Speeding and overly large PMAs have also caused anxiety and concern.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We need these new rules to improve path safety, especially for vulnerable users, like young children and seniors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Ms Jean See and Ms Poh Li San asked for an update on the new rules, while Mr Eric Chua asked how we can improve path safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To implement the rules, we need to amend legislation and we are scheduled to do so through Parliament later this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will provide sufficient transition time for users and other stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I will now share more details on how we plan to implement the new PMA rules.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The exact timeline will depend on when we can amend legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Six kilometres per hour is the same speed as a brisk walker, so that is a reasonable top speed allowable since PMAs are meant for those with walking difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will make it an offence to display, advertise and sell PMAs exceeding the dimension limits, or with device speed limit above six kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Based on checks with several retailers, many have already stopped selling such PMAs or are clearing limited stock.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, they must be used safely within the new speed limit of six kilometres per hour and comply with the upcoming dimension limits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To monitor the speed, PMA users may take reference from the walking speeds of other path users or use a physical speedometer or mobile application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Third, only those with genuine medical needs will be allowed to use a mobility scooter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since last year, we have engaged stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, to develop a certification process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: MOH will engage and provide guidelines to the medical community ahead of implementation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This requirement for certification does not apply to motorised wheelchair users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Under AMS, users with medical conditions which result in mobility difficulties will be certified to need a mobility scooter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Before the commencement of AMS, those who were prescribed a mobility scooter subsidised by the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund (SMF), under the Agency for Integrated Care; or the Assistive Technology Fund (ATF) under SG Enable, will automatically be certified without having to do anything.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Individuals with an existing non-subsidised mobility scooter or who intend to obtain a mobility scooter, should visit their regular doctor for an AMS.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Those purchasing an SMF- or ATF-subsidised mobility scooter for the first time should obtain an AMS through their regular doctor or Occupational Therapist at their existing touchpoints.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For most new SMF or ATF clients, AMS will not add any extra steps to the current subsidy application process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: From the first quarter of 2026, mobility scooter users on public paths must have this certification of need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will give users some time to obtain the certification, and enforcement officers will engage and educate users on the new rules during this transition period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users do not have to approach healthcare professionals to obtain certification now.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Please wait for more details to be released in the third quarter of this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We understand that some genuine PMA users who do deliveries are concerned that the reduced speed limit will affect earnings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Together with delivery platforms and the National Delivery Champions Association, we have just issued a joint statement on this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The delivery platforms have given assurance that they will continue to be inclusive on their platforms, in terms of job allocation and managing customer expectations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In addition, the Government will continue working with stakeholders to enhance the infrastructure and processes supporting last-mile deliveries at developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Taken together, we hope these new rules will curb the misuse of PMAs and improve safety for all path users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan raised concerns on safety risks from non-compliant motorised Personal Mobility Devices (PMDs) and Power-Assisted Bicycles (PABs), both the device itself and its use on public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the years, we have put in place stringent measures and safety standards to mitigate the risks of motorised PMDs and PABs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our enforcement officers conduct operations daily against non-compliant devices on paths and we take action against retailers selling non-compliant devices or those that illegally modify devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, challenges remain with online sales and illegal modifications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have observed incidents in other cities where such devices caught fire on public transport, resulting in injuries and the banning of such devices from public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Dennis Tan raised feedback on inconsiderate commuters who eat and drink, play loud music and pose a nuisance to other commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In more egregious cases, some harass others and even challenge our bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Public transport is a shared space and such behaviour affects the commuting experience for everyone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At worst, it can make people feel unsafe about travelling on public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have therefore increased patrolling and enforcement against such offences on both trains and buses, and will be strengthening our regulatory powers to act against inconsiderate behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At present, our regulatory power to manage commuter behaviour onboard buses is more limited than on rail.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As a first step, we are working with our public bus operators to put in place Conditions of Carriage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These conditions will provide for a safe and comfortable experience for commuters and bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It will set out what transport workers can do to alleviate situations with uncooperative commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In egregious cases, bus captains can instruct disruptive commuters to alight from the bus, or if necessary, activate the Police.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Those who behave egregiously will face penalties commensurate with the severity of their impact on other commuters, with higher penalties for repeat offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We recognise that some cases involved commuters who may be experiencing a mental health episode and what they need is support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our officers will exercise discretion in applying these regulations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To complement these, we will continue to promote gracious journeys, with more signages and public announcements to encourage positive behaviour, such as keeping volumes low and occupying only one seat.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Commuters can also make journeys more gracious by looking out for those in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In 2023, I had announced the expansion of the "Helping Hand" scheme, with cards indicating, for example, a commuter’s need for a seat.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Recognising that commuters have different needs we will be launching a universal Helping Hand card with a blank space where commuters can write their specific needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will be in addition to the earlier issued cards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: With these measures, I hope that all commuters will play their part in fostering safer and more gracious journeys.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Just as we rejuvenate older estates, we want to make sure that commuter infrastructure keeps pace with changing needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, after the completion of the Woodlands Extension in 1996, the total daily ridership for the North-South and East-West lines stood at about 900,000.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, that number has grown to 1.6 million.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our infrastructure must also be inclusive, especially for seniors and those who need more assistance with navigation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have continually improved our MRT stations over the years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Certain high-traffic stations, like City Hall and Raffles Place, are undergoing enhancements, such as new lighting and air-conditioning systems, upgraded toilets and clearer signages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: When a new line connects to an existing station, we improve pedestrian walkways and include new entrances and exits for better accessibility and crowd management.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, when linking Orchard station along the North-South Line with the Thomson-East Coast Line, we installed more escalators and travellators and new entrances serving surrounding malls.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Besides nearby transport nodes, we also endeavour to provide covered linkways from new stations to key developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We seek Mr Lim Biow Chuan’s understanding that these sometimes come after new stations are opened, as more time is needed to address differing stakeholder requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Beyond these station improvements that have taken place over time, we are planning for a refresh of our North-South/East-West Line stations to accommodate increasing ridership and to ensure a more seamless, comfortable commute.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will study how the positive lessons from the newest Thomson-East Coast Line, which has been well received by commuters, can be applied to older stations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These improvements could include making stations more accessible, with additional escalators and lifts; improving navigation, with better wayfinding signages; and making our spaces more pleasant, with upgraded amenities like toilets and services for commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We are currently looking at Yishun station as our first case study.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Yishun is one of our older North-South Line stations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In recent years, the station has become busier and we expect more commuters as surrounding developments are completed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will study whether the station platform can be extended to ease crowding during peak hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We may add escalators, lifts and access points to facilitate the flow of commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will also explore how we can improve the transfer experience, with upgrades to the bus stop, drop-off point and taxi stand, and new covered linkways to enhance shelter to nearby locations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Beyond these infrastructural enhancements, we also want to re-imagine public transport spaces to better serve commuters and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, the new Punggol Coast Station on the North-East Line has a civic common space where residents, students from the Singapore Institute of Technology and people working in the Punggol Digital District can enjoy and interact.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our public transport operators have already been working with the communities to improve the vibrancy of stations and interchanges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will find opportunities to create more vibrant spaces such as by repurposing underutilised areas to support community and commercial uses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: More details will be shared when our studies are completed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, now let me now say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: From the fourth quarter of this year, users can visit their regular doctor to obtain this certification of medical need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will release more details in the third quarter of this year and provide sufficient transition time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users do not have to approach healthcare professionals to obtain certification now.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This requirement for certification is only for mobility scooter users and does not apply to motorised wheelchair users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We hope that these rules will ensure that PMAs are used responsibly, improving path safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We also hope that commuters enjoy a safe and comfortable journey on public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Unfortunately, we have been receiving increased feedback on inconsiderate commuter behaviour on public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This includes commuters consuming food and drink, or playing loud music or videos on their mobile devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some commuters have even soiled our train stations, or harassed others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Thus, to maintain a positive travel experience for commuters, we will be strengthening our regulatory powers to act against inconsiderate behaviour, with the penalty increasing for repeat offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We hope that all commuters will play their part to be considerate and foster more comfortable and pleasant journeys. : Mr Chairman, in conclusion, we will continue making journeys on public transport and public paths safer and more comfortable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We look forward to the support of commuters in understanding and abiding by the regulations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Together, let us build a more gracious commuter culture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The other good news is about the Seletar Line and Tengah Line going through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As he mentioned, hopefully, it will through Toa Payoh, and not only Toa Payoh but Toa Payoh East as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My first question, Mr Chairman, is in regard to Senior Minister of State Amy Khor's speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: She mentioned about the extension of the areas around schools.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Because originally, it was only during school hours.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But as you mentioned, the school hours are becoming a bit more adaptable and dynamic, so, whether there will be enhanced cameras, surveillance and monitoring systems, and whether we will be working with other agencies to enhance that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Because the safety of our children and our students is very important, and I am very particular about that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second, to Minister of State Murali, he mentioned about the public bus safety review.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: He highlighted, very importantly, that driving a bus is like flying a plane, if I am not mistaken.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My third question, Mr Chairman, is in terms of Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey's speech earlier about medical certification or certificate of needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I just want to clarify whether the cost will be free.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Some of them may already have medical certification before, so, whether there be some leeway in terms of cost issues for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Because he mentioned that more details will be announced after third quarter, some of them be concerned about how they can expect to apply for this certificate of need and how they will apply for them with the doctors; and whether there are cost issues concerned, whether existing ones can actually travel, can be applied going forward.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi, your three short clarifications are not so short.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I can understand why he made that comparison.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And for those who do not meet the means testing requirements, they need to pay a fee for the doctors to give them the certification.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: More details will be released by MOH later this year, so we urge potential users to look out for that.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the extension of the lower speed limit to school zones for full day, we will work with the relevant agencies on the enhanced enforcements.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, there will be clear signages and so on to let motorists know that the lower speed limit is for the full day, as well as, of course, work with the various stakeholders like the schools and the residents in the area.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, I am going to request all Members to really keep it short and, likewise, the answers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: I want to thank Minister Chee, the Senior Minister of State, Minister of State and Senior Parliamentary Secretary for their very detailed explanation of the Budget for next year.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: In your view, what is the key enabler or enablers, I should say, that will ensure Singapore remains a leading global supply chain hub.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Neil Parekh for his question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think this is an important topic to focus on, especially in our current environment where we see more volatility and more disruptions to trade flows and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What are the key enablers that will ensure that Singapore can retain our competitive advantage?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I did say in my speech earlier, Mr Chairman, that we must not assume that our current hub status and our competitive advantage will be there forever.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The competition is very intense and we do need to make sure that we continue to improve, to upgrade our capabilities to be able to meet with this rising competition.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are a few key enablers in my mind that I think would be critical.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a key strength for Singapore, and the tripartite partners – the employers, the unions, the Government – we work closely together to achieve a win-win outcome for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is something which allows us to be able to overcome obstacles, deal with crisis, including during COVID-19, and to be able to seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, I would say one of our advantages is to be able to work as an ecosystem in an integrated manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we do not just work in silos.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We bring the stakeholders together, and whether it is within the Government, across different Government agencies, or with the private sector and the unions, we are able to then look at what will be the best solution as a whole and maximise our collective strength.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, long-term planning, because many of these capabilities, whether is it hardware, infrastructure, skills upgrading, you cannot ramp up at the last minute.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, because of that, this element in our process, in the way we work, long-term planning, I think will be quite critical, and you can see that in our planning for Terminal 5 and for Tuas Port, And I will add a last one, which I think is an area that we need to continue to work on, which is to use the three advantages that I mentioned earlier – tripartism, our ecosystem integration, and with the ability to plan long term – to also look at how we can continuously review and improve our regulatory environment for businesses, to reduce regulatory burdens, business costs, to be able to support new technologies and innovations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I have a clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The Minister announced that there will be new bus services under the Bus Enhancement Plan this year, in 2025, but none of these services will ply Jurong West.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And we know the Jurong Regional Line will only come to Jurong in two to three years' time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, I hope the Minister can add new services in Jurong West this year, especially linking the residents to essential services like polyclinics, and not have to walk 170 metres.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The second question is on the upgrading of bus stops.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Many existing bus stops in Jurong West are old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, may I know what is LTA's plan and timeline for upgrading the bus stops in Singapore, including those in Jurong West?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I want to assure Mr Ang that we will certainly follow up with him and his team in Jurong West to take a look at what are the areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Bus stops, I will also ask LTA to follow up with Mr Ang.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, I believe my concerns with regard to the deployment of autonomous buses in Singapore were not addressed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: So, can I ask the Minister to provide an update on the plans to deploy these autonomous buses and what is the road map?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How many public transport workers, in particular, the bus captains and the bus technicians, will be affected in such a roll-out?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Are there any plans to ensure that the affected workers are suitably upskilled, reskilled and redeployed in advance?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Melvin Yong and the union leaders from NTWU have been working very closely with us on the autonomous vehicles pilot.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have launched a Request for Proposal in January to purchase autonomous buses for this pilot and we intend to award the contract by the end of this year, and so to get the pilot started, and then we can learn from the experience as we go along, both from the operator's point of view, but also from the union's point of view and then to see what we can do together to give assurance to our workers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I think the Minister may have misunderstood the spirit or the thrust of my question in my Budget debate speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Basically, in essence, I was asking how will we step up in the next few years to mitigate any increase in the aviation emissions arising from the opening of T5 with the increase in the number of flights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: And I just want to make a clarification regarding what I said about Heathrow.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I was not talking about now, but it is 11%.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I did say 10% but I could have made a mistake mixing it up with the UK government's mandate for sustainable aviation fuel to hit the target of 10% by 2030.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Likewise, I think there are also other countries like Japan which is also aiming for 10% by 2030.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, I do hope and I would support Singapore's effort to continue for its mitigation efforts to deal with the aviation emissions even as we expand our airport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I first want to thank Mr Tan for his clarification and for stating clearly his position that he supports the development of T5 and for our air hub at Changi to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I wanted to thank Mr Tan for that indeed because the competitiveness of our air hub is one of the goals.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Speaker, I just wanted to point out that my question relating to safety of occupational drivers was not responded to.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: So, could I perhaps ask the Minister of State what are actually the Ministry's plans in working with stakeholders to reinforce the shared responsibility for safety of occupational drivers, who could be PHV drivers as well as heavy vehicle drivers?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As the hon Member would appreciate, my focus or at least my task force's focus, was really looking at the bus captains in the public transport arena, and not in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And perhaps it is time to visit these recommendations with them and see what can be taken on board.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: The Minister mentioned an additional $1 billion on top of the existing $5 billion top-up to support Changi Airport's expansion and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Could you share on the measures or initiatives that will enable smaller enterprises, especially SMEs, to enable them to tap into new business opportunities arising as Changi continues to grow?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Mr Chairman, I think when we invest in growing our airhub, there will be direct and indirect benefits that will flow to the ecosystem, including our local companies, our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: So, I do not want to be too specific because really depends on how they intend to execute some of these plans, but broadly, I would say, on infrastructure, because that was one of the areas that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: When we build infrastructure, I think there will be opportunities to involve some of our local companies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Some of them may be big enough to take on the contracts as the main contractor, but some of them may not be big enough, but they can pair up with the bigger companies, whether local or foreign.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: And then they can participate in the process as well and build up their track records.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I think we also have some good local companies that have good technology solutions to offer and I think they can help to optimise the airport operations, including whether there are ways to improve environmental sustainability, as what Mr Tan mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I think these are also areas that we can involve the local companies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Because skills upgrading will be important, some of our local SMEs are also involved in this space as training providers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: So, I think that will also be another possible area that they can benefit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But my point is actually that this duration is arbitrary and we needlessly tie ourselves to a legacy duration that may be misaligned with what will be reasonable in terms of a key component of an EV, which is the battery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor has indicated that a system of multiple COE durations could become unwieldy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Although, of course, now we seem to manage a two-duration system with no issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But based on what MOT has already announced, it will anyhow phase out the issuance of internal combustion engine (ICE)-COE starting in 2030 and the local fleet will be all EV by 2040.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If so, would a change in duration not be considered at this later point in the future?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have noted in my reply and as the learned Assoc Prof has also said, definitely the validity period of the COE is not tied to the lifespan of the vehicle.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Actually, as I have said, it is really for greater equity, so that motorist do not own a car in perpetuity at the expense of future car owners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, this 10-year period really is a good balance between certainty for existing owners and a good chance, a chance for somebody who may wish to purchase a car.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And it also happens to tie-in with the time limit for the PARF benefits, which is actually, to encourage vehicle fleet renewal in Singapore, is still relevant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And as I have said, we have been using this validity period, monitoring.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They did not think that the cars would last for more than five years and we gave a concession for the five-year renewal.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, the system has not really got multiple COE validity periods.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And as I have said, actually, we are technology agnostic, too, in the sense that technology evolves.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We want cleaner energy vehicles, but it does not have to be EV, although at this point in time, EV is the most viable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Warranty, eight years, but some companies are already giving 10 years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, I think it is not really sensible to tie it to a specific technology.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Ms Ng Ling Ling, I am sorry we have run out of time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, can I invite Mr Saktiandi Supaat if you would like to draw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to highlight that I am thankful to all the 19 Members and who have asked questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We have 55 questions for MOT this year; which is almost 30% to 35% increase from last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is a testament to the work that MOT and the One Transport Family has been doing for the past year and going forward as well, given that the work is not just for this year, but also for many decades down the road.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Minister Chee Hong Tat, Senior Minister of State, Minister of State, Senior Parliamentary Secretary and, of course, the One Transport Family, all the staff, including those from LTA, MPA, CAAS; and as Minister mentioned, the importance of our tripartite partners to make sure that MOT work and Singapore is well taken care of.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On that note, Mr Chairman, I seek leave to withdraw my amendment.
